newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH PM'S PARTY SEEN TOPPING SENATE VOTE-ANALYST.
newsitem.headline: CZECH PM'S PARTY SEEN TOPPING SENATE VOTE-ANALYST.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) is likely to fare best in the first Senate elections scheduled for later this month, an independent polling expert said on Tuesday.

On the basis of results of a survey conducted by the independent public opinion agency Factum, the position of ODS's biggest rival, the opposition Social Democrats (CSSD), had weakened, Factum director Jan Herzmann said.

The poll conducted in mid-October among 1,064 Czechs showed ODS being by supported by 25.4 percent, up from 23.7 in September, while CSSD has declined to 20.2 percent from 24.4, but it did not project how many seats each party would win.

The Senate, the new upper chamber of Czech parliament which will have limited legislative powers, is to be elected in a first-past-the-post poll in 81 separate constituencies in two rounds on November 15-16 and November 22-23.
But Herzmann said voters will tend to choose the candidate by the party he or she represents rather than vote on an individual's merits.
Factum said in a separate poll released on Monday that after an inconclusive first round 79 ODS candidates and 73 CSSD candidates were likely to fight in a second round for control of the Senate.
The Senate vote will be the first key test for the centre-right three-party coalition which lost its majority in the lower house when the CSSD posted a strong second place in June general elections.

A crucial blow for CSSD came when four of its deputies broke party ranks to provide the margin for the approval of the government's draft 1997 budget last month in its first reading, against the wishes of the Social Democrats' leadership.
"Disputes in CSSD ... weakened its position as an alternative to ODS, and ODS is likely to win the elections," Herzmann told a news conference on Tuesday.

The survey showed the junior coalition partner, the Christian and Democratic Union (KDU-CSL), dropped to 7.7 percent from 8.0 in the previous poll, while the other partner Civic Democratic Aliance (ODA) rose to 6.8 from 5.9.

Another opposition party, the Communists (KSCM) rose to 9.5 from 8.4 percent. The third subject in the oppostion, the ultra-right Republicans (SPR-RSC) were not included in the survey since the party is boycotting the races.
As another factor pointing to ODS's success, Herzmann sees a stable electoral base for the party.
He said the Factum survey showed 77.4 percent of voters identified as traditional voters of ODS would stay with the party, compared with 66.3 percent for CSSD.

In the second round, into which only two most succesful candidates per consituency go, ODS is likely to receive support from its coaliton partners' voters, while CSSD is not that far acceptable for KSCM and SPR-RSC supporters, he noted.

The survey showed 48 percent of ODA voters and 41.9 of KDU-CSL voters were satisfied with ODS as the strongest party of the ruling colation. On the other hand 24.6 percent of KSCM voters and 20.7 percent of SPR-RSC voters are happy with the way CSSD works as the strongest opposition party.
"We can expect low election attendance which in the first round would be slightly above 50 percent and in the second round even under 50 percent," Herzmann said.
ODS voters have a stronger interest in voting in the Senate elections, the poll showed, with 78.3 percent of ODS supporters saying they would vote compared to 64.6 percent of CSSD voters.
